b: The first time I held a cordless tool, other than a drill, was around 1984. The engineer at a radio station I was working at brought in his new Makita 7.2-volt jigsaw. The idea of cutting wood without a cord blew me away, and I wasted no time getting one.

The specs on that first battery were modest: 7.2 nominal volts, 1.3Ah storing 9.4Wh of energy, and a weight of less than a pound. Of course, technology moved fast, and the batteries — and their associated power — started growing.

Now, not quite 45 years later, we’re talking about 18/20-volt batteries* with a capacity of 15Ah, packing energy of 270Wh — some 29 times the energy of that old Makita, but only about three or four times the weight.

Until this year only one major company offered one of these batteries, DeWalt. Its 20V/60V FlexVolt battery established the 15Ah category in 2021 and has held it largely to itself since then. But earlier this year, Bosch entered the playing field with the company’s Expert18V 15Ah unit. Now, Milwaukee has just joined the club with their M18 RedLithium Forge 15HD battery.

The three batteries share most of their specs: 18/20 volts, 15Ah, and 270Wh, with each battery being compatible with the respective company’s full line of cordless tools of that voltage. The main area where the specs aren’t similar is battery weight. Both the Bosch and the new Milwaukee weigh in at around 3-1/2 lbs., with the older DeWalt a heftier 4-1/2 lbs.

Too heavy for a cordless tool? Well, if you’re snapping one of these into a drill/driver to install drywall ceilings for a few hours, heck yeah. But for cordless tools you don’t have to handle while using, such as jobsite table saws, miter saws, compressors or vacuums, the weight isn’t really an issue.
What the issue is, is the fact that cordless technology keeps getting better, more powerful, and closer to the promise of replacing corded tools.
*Depending on the nomenclature used by the manufacturer. Both have nominal voltage of 18 volts.
